html:
A time of prosperity in Peru in the mid 1800s, paid for by selling guano, the dried droppings of seabirds, as fertiliser. On rainless islands off the coast, such as the Chincha Islands, guano had piled up for thousands of years, in places many metres deep.

Andean farmers had long used it. In the 1840s European and American farmers discovered it too, as their soils wore out. Peru's state owned the deposits and sold the rights to merchant houses, such as the British firm Antony Gibbs and Sons. Under president Ramón Castilla, guano money paid for:

  • the end of slavery and of the Indigenous head tax, in 1854
  • railways, the army and a growing government
  • loans from abroad, which grew into large debts

The digging was brutal work, done by convicts and, increasingly, Chinese indentured workers brought on harsh contracts. Spain seized the Chincha Islands in 1864. When the guano ran low, Peru turned to nitrates, which led to the War of the Pacific with Chile.
